title: What Fear Makes Us Not Do
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Kathleen Schafer asks why leaders and communities struggle to listen to reason when emotions run high, and argues that discernment is a practice that must be cultivated before the crisis arrives. Her central example is Senator Russ Feingold's lone vote against the USA PATRIOT Act in October 2001, which she treats as a model of trusting what one sees while ninety-eight others move the other way. From there she widens the lens to organizations, families, and communities, which all need people willing to name what is not working and cultures of trust that let them speak. Her key distinction is that fear is information, not direction: it rightly signals threat but narrows vision and craves certainty and blame. She offers a set of diagnostic questions for decision-making and grounds them in her work on Citizen Leadership, where knowledge held by frontline people often exceeds that of those with titles. The essay closes with a simple test for fast decisions: ask whether fear is driving this.
points: Schafer uses Feingold's 98 to 1 dissent on the PATRIOT Act as an example of the courage to question a unanimous, fear-driven rush.
She argues that in most organizational failures someone knew something was wrong but either stayed silent or was ignored.
Her core distinction is that fear is useful information about threat but a poor guide to direction.
She offers a practical test for rapid decisions: not whether fear is present, but whether fear is driving the choice.
quotes: In almost every example I encounter that creates havoc in an organization, someone knew something wasn't right. Sometimes they didn't share what they knew. Other times they did and were ignored.

I think part of the answer is that discernment requires practice. Without a mindful practice of leadership, without ways of staying connected to what we know, what we value and what we are actually trying to create, it becomes remarkably easy to lose sight of our own power to recognize truth and act on it.
Ninety-eight people are moving in one direction and one person remained willing to trust what he was seeing enough to question it.
The question is whether we have created enough trust for people to speak
Fear serves a purpose. It tells us something feels threatening and deserves our attention. But fear is not particularly good at determining where we should go next.
The person closest to the problem may know something the person with the title does not. The frontline employee may see the system more clearly than the executive.
That is different from asking whether fear is present. Sometimes there is very good reason to be afraid. But decisions made primarily from fear rarely age well.
